sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for? No.** The page title "Rainfall at the reservoir" (x 120–480, y 55–90) promises rainfall data. The chart under it (x 120–640, y 136–495) has three bars and no labels, values, units, or time period, so it says nothing. The only content anyone can actually read is "Getting there" (x 704–1065, y 140–280), which covers the number twelve bus, parking, and cycle racks. A viewer can't tell whether this is a rainfall report or a visitor's guide, and leaves with travel directions under a title about weather. A page should be self-evident at a glance (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*). Here the reader has to work out how the parts relate, and the page doesn't give enough to do it. Fix: decide what the page is for and make the title say that. If it's a visitor page, use a title like "Visiting the reservoir" with "Rainfall" and "Getting there" as equal sections below it. If it's a rainfall page, the directions belong somewhere else. The chart then needs labels to carry any meaning, which belongs to the Charts section. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Does each heading name what its section holds? No.** The H1 "Rainfall at the reservoir" sits over both columns, so it reads as the heading for the whole page. Half of the page under it is about transport. The chart column has no heading of its own, while "Getting there" (704,150) does. That makes the hierarchy uneven: one column is headed by the page title and the other by its own subheading. A reader scanning the headings gets the wrong idea of what the page contains (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6, headings describe their section). Fix: give the page a title that covers both sections, and give the chart a heading at the same level as "Getting there" that names what it shows, for example "Rainfall, last three months". Convention. Weight: major. It's tied to finding 1, and the director may merge the two.
3. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job? No.** The chart sits in a dark grey frame about 3 px thick with a pale blue fill (x 120–640, y 136–495). The frame is the heaviest line on the page, heavier than the baseline and the type, and it draws the eye to the edge of the chart instead of the bars. Space already separates the chart from the text column, so the frame separates nothing. A plain chart would lose nothing. Tufte calls lines like this, which carry no information, non-data ink (*The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 4–5). Fix: remove the border and keep at most the pale tone, or let white space alone set the chart apart (Lupton, *Thinking with Type*). Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The type, colours, and shapes all come from one family: a single sans-serif, one blue, near-black text, and plain rectangles. The page reads as one restrained piece, not a collage, so fixing the content and structure won't mean restyling anything.
- The copy in "Getting there" is finished and concrete: a route number, a frequency, a time of day, and a landmark. Each sentence tells a visitor something they can act on.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 5 yes, 3 no (purpose clear in one sentence; every element does a job; each heading names its section)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One point outside the checklist lines, which I judged as taste: the only subheading on the page, "Getting there" (≈704,140), sits on the travel note, which looks like the secondary content. The chart (120–640, 136–495) is the main content and has no heading, caption or label of its own, so it depends on the page title "Rainfall at the reservoir" (120,55) to explain it. Because of this, the order of the words says "the travel note is a titled section" while the order of the shapes says "the chart is what matters". Giving the chart its own heading, at the same level as "Getting there", would make the two agree. I'm passing this on so you can decide whether it matters. It is not a "no" on any line.

**What's working.**
- There is one obvious place to start. The chart block is the heaviest thing on the page. It is about 520×360 px of solid blue on a pale tint inside a dark frame. The eye lands on it at once and then goes up to the title, which is the right order for a page about rainfall.
- The text has three levels that are easy to tell apart. The title looks like about 30 px bold, "Getting there" about 21 px bold, and the body about 17 px regular. Each step changes both size and weight, so the heading doesn't blur into the body even though their sizes are close. The bold weight separates them, as Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*, recommend ("bolder, not bigger").

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The type sizes are estimated by eye. No measured facts file was given, and my shell commands were refused, so I couldn't zoom in with the crop script. At 1280×800 the image is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. If the sizes matter, measure "Getting there" and the body text: if the heading turns out to be within about 2 px of the body, the second line would become a "no".

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?** The "Getting there" column (x≈704–1080, y≈140–275) sits right beside the rainfall chart (x 120–639, y 137–495). Its top lines up with the box top, and both sit under the one title "Rainfall at the reservoir" (y≈55–90). Side by side under one heading, the two read as one unit: chart plus explanation. A viewer looks to the paragraph for what the bars mean and gets bus times and parking instead. That costs them a second read and leaves the chart looking unexplained. Placing things together is a promise that they belong together (Wertheimer; Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II; Gestalt grouping). Fix: separate the two by space and structure. Either give the travel information its own region and heading level, clearly apart from the rainfall section (for example below it, after a larger gap, or in a visibly separate sidebar), or give the chart's column text that actually explains the rainfall. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over?** and **Does the visual weight balance, with no side that makes the page look about to tip?** All the content sits in the top-left of the frame. The heaviest element is the dark-bordered, tinted chart box on the left, and the right column is just four light lines of text. Under that text is a leftover pocket (x≈704–1080, y≈280–495), and the bottom band (y≈495–800, about 38% of the frame) is empty. The right margin (~200 px) doesn't match the left (120 px). The empty areas look like what was left over, not like space shaped against the content, so the page feels unfinished and leans to the upper left (Ruder, *Typography*, "Contrasts"; Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Fix: decide what the open space is for. Either let the content fill the frame (match the right margin to the left, let the text column take its share, place the next content below) or gather the emptiness into one clearly intended field. If more page follows below this capture, the bottom band matters less, but the pocket and the uneven margins still do. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The title and the chart box share one left edge (x=120), and the chart's top lines up with the right column's top. That gives a clean two-column structure with a single gutter of about 64 px. Keep it when regrouping.
- Inside the right column, "Getting there" sits tight to its paragraph (about 10 px) and well away from the title (about 50 px), so that heading clearly belongs to its own text.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (only related elements look alike; empty space gathered; visual weight balances), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies. The heading "Rainfall at the reservoir", the subhead "Getting there" and one four-line paragraph. The chart has no text, so there's nothing in it to check here.

**Findings**
None.

The only line I was unsure about was line length. The paragraph at x≈704–1062, y≈175–278 runs about 39–42 characters a line, which is a little under 45. The catalog entry is about lines that run too wide, and it gives 40 to 50 characters for text set in several columns (Bringhurst, 2.1.2). This paragraph sits as a second column next to the chart, so the length is fine. The answer is yes.

A note for the director, outside this section: the paragraph is about transport, while the title and chart are about rainfall. Whether that mismatch is a problem belongs to the whole-piece and hierarchy critics.

**What's working.**
- The type plan is clean. It uses one sans family, and each level has a clear job. The title (~34 px bold) sits well above the subhead (~21 px semibold), which sits above the body (~17 px regular). Each step is a big jump, so nothing reads as a near-miss.
- The paragraph is easy to read. It's near-black on white, set flush left with an even rag, and the line spacing (~1.6) suits the short lines.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The page has a neutral range (near-black text, a gray frame and baseline, a white page) and one blue, used on the bars and as a pale tint behind the chart.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Small palette, with the strong color only where the content is.** The one saturated blue appears only on the three bars (about x 183–527, y 207–453), and they make up a small share of the page. Everything else is neutral or a pale tint of the same blue. So the bars are the only strong color, and the eye goes to the data first. Keep it to this one hue if more content is added.
- **Clear range from light to dark.** The page goes from white, to the very pale blue panel, to the mid-gray frame, to the dark blue bars and the near-black headings. In grayscale the panel, bars and text would still separate cleanly, so the structure doesn't depend on hue.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so no crops were needed. The only graphic is an unlabeled bar chart in a framed panel at about x 120–640, y 136–495. That belongs to the Charts and data section, not Pictures, so this section stops after step 1.

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. There are no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks; the only graphic is a bar chart, which the `data` section covers.

None.

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one bar chart (one series, three bars) at about x 120–639, y 137–495.

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart name what its marks show, with axis values, units, and series labels?** (This also covers the `no` answers to "Is each series label placed at its data rather than in a separate legend?", "Are categorical bars sorted by value or by a natural order?" and "Does each chart show enough of the time range or sample to judge the trend?") The chart has no text at all: no y-axis or tick values, no unit, and no names under the three bars (x about 183–271, 311–399, 439–527, all on the baseline at y 453).
   - **What the viewer meets:** three blue shapes. The second is tallest and the third is shortest. They can't tell whether the bars are months, years or rain gauges, whether the tallest is 40 mm or 400 mm, or whether this is a normal year. That means they can't check whether the order (medium, tall, short) is a time order or arbitrary, or whether three bars are enough to judge any trend. The chart only shows that the amounts differ, which is almost nothing.
   - **Why:** Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 2: the reader should never have to guess what a number measures. Few, *Show Me the Numbers*: sort bars by value or by a natural order.
   - **Fix direction:**
     - Name each bar directly under it, with the period or place.
     - Give the values, either as a light y-axis with the unit (mm) or as a figure printed on each bar.
     - Add the period covered and the source.
     - If the bars are time periods, keep them in time order and say so. If they are not, sort them by value.
     - If the point is a trend, show enough periods for a trend to show.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major.

2. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** The only text tied to the chart is the page heading "Rainfall at the reservoir" (y about 55–90). It names the topic, not what the data shows, and there is no caption or text alternative.
   - **What the viewer meets:** with no labels as well, they are given no takeaway at all, and a screen-reader user gets nothing.
   - **Why:** the catalog's source for this one is not on the approved list, so it rests on common sense. A chart with no stated point leaves every reader to work it out, and here they can't. A text alternative for an informative chart is also expected under WCAG.
   - **Fix direction:** add a caption that states the finding, for example which period was wettest and by how much compared with normal. Make sure the chart has a text alternative carrying the same point.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major.

3. **Is nearly all the ink in each chart data, with no 3D, shadows, textures, or heavy gridlines?** The chart sits in a dark slate frame that looks about 3 px thick (x 120–639, y 137–495) on a pale blue panel.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the frame is as dark as anything in the chart and heavier than the 1–2 px baseline. It boxes the chart off as an object instead of a reading, and it spends ink on the box while the data has none of its labels.
   - **Why:** Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, 23.2, and Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 5: support lines should not be as strong as the data.
   - **Fix direction:** remove the frame, or make it a thin pale grey, so the bars are the strongest marks. The pale panel tint can stay if the layout needs it.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One flat, solid blue for the one series.** There are no gradients, 3D or spurious extra colours. The bars look comfortably above 3:1 contrast against the panel, so the encoding is clean. Keep it when the labels go in.
- **The bars stand on one shared baseline, with even widths and gaps.** Lengths can be compared directly by position on a common scale, which suits a comparison.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the baseline is zero. There is no value axis, so this has to be confirmed in the source data or chart settings.
- Whether a text alternative exists in the markup.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 11 yes, 5 no (ink nearly all data; enough of the time range or sample; series labels at the data; axis values, units, and series labels; title or caption states the finding). The fifth `no`, bars sorted by value or a natural order, is folded into finding 1.

I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop script, but at 1280×800 the image is one screen and needs no crops.

**Section.** Interface: skipped. The image has no buttons, links, fields, menus or navigation. It holds only a heading, a bar chart in a bordered panel and a paragraph of text. The panel's border frames the chart and does not suggest that it can be clicked.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Interface: skipped
